content.overview: Section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines transfer of property as an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself and one or more other living persons. Company or association or body of individuals is treated as a living person for this section. Wills and other dispositions taking effect only on death are outside this definition.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Living person to living person? (2) Conveyance in present or future? (3) Not a will? (4) Which named mode follows (sale, mortgage, lease, gift)?
content.study:
s. 5 is the definitional gateway. Named modes — sale (s. 54), mortgage (s. 58), lease (s. 105), gift (s. 122) — operate within this concept.

No case holdings invented. Case-law verification remains a separate gate.

sections.heading: Living person
sections.body: Transferor and transferee must be living persons; company/association/body of individuals counts as a living person under the section.

sections.heading: Conveyance
sections.body: Property may be conveyed in present or in future.

sections.heading: Wills excluded
sections.body: Dispositions taking effect only on death (wills) are not transfers under s. 5.

sections.heading: Named modes
sections.body: Sale, mortgage, lease and gift are the principal statutory modes that follow.

sections.heading: Routing
sections.body: Identify the mode, then open the corresponding section topic.

examples.title: Company as living person
examples.body: A company conveys land by registered sale deed — treated as a living person under s. 5; mode is sale under s. 54.

hypotheticals.question: Is a will a transfer under s. 5?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. A will takes effect on death and is outside the living-person conveyance defined in s. 5.

distinctions.title: s. 5 transfer vs will
distinctions.left: Living person conveys inter vivos (present or future).

misconceptions.trap: Every property disposition is a TPA transfer under s. 5.
misconceptions.correction: Wills and purely testamentary dispositions are outside s. 5.
